What is at stake

The Kingdom's future rests on water, green cover and stable land.

All four are under pressure. All four are hard to watch at national scale from the ground.

Water 10.8 bn m³

Non-renewable groundwater drawn in 2023. This fossil water does not refill. Every hidden leak and every over-watered field spends a reserve the next generation cannot replace.

Green cover 151 M

Trees planted by mid-2025, on the way to ten billion. The investment only counts if the trees survive their first summers, and survival is still mostly checked on foot.

Land & sand 40 M ha

Degraded land the Kingdom aims to restore. Moving sand buries new plantings, farms, roads and rail. Bare, disturbed soil sends dust into cities.

Mountain forests 11–15%

Share of juniper trees with dieback in Asir and Al-Baha in a field study of the southwest. These are ancient forests on steep slopes that ground teams reach slowly.

The visibility gap

Satellites see the region. Field teams see a few hectares. Nobody sees every tree.

A Sentinel-2 satellite pixel covers 10 × 10 metres, roughly the space of nine young seedlings, and returns one value for all of them. Field crews see each tree but cover only a small area per day, so the first sign of a failed drip line is often a row of dead trees.

EMYRGEN aircraft fly the same sites every few weeks at centimetre detail, find each tree again by its coordinates, and report exactly what changed.

The technology

One system, from sensor to verified result.

Every mission follows the same six steps. Nothing is closed until a later flight confirms the problem is fixed.

STEP 1

Fly

The aircraft flies a pre-approved route on its own. RTK satellite positioning places every image to within a few centimetres, so the same tree is found again on every flight.

STEP 2

Sense

Swappable sensor payloads are chosen per mission: plant-health camera, thermal camera, laser scanner, high-resolution camera, dust and weather probes.

STEP 3

Flag in flight

An onboard computer spots urgent findings during the flight, such as a dry drip line, a fire or a broken fence, and sends them by radio or satellite link.

STEP 4

Analyse

Processing inside the Kingdom builds the map, counts every tree, scores its health and compares it with the previous flight.

STEP 5

Act

The operations dashboard turns findings into work orders with coordinates, priority and the responsible team, sent to field crews' phones.

STEP 6

Verify

The next flight checks the same trees. The work order closes only when the result is confirmed, with before-and-after evidence on file.

DATA

Maps and records are hosted on infrastructure inside the Kingdom and owned by the Saudi program. Outputs use standard mapping formats (GeoTIFF, GeoJSON, shapefile), so they load directly into the GIS tools government teams already use.

The sensors, and what each one finds in the Kingdom

Plant-health camera

Measures
Light in 5–10 bands, including red-edge and near-infrared. Gives vigour indices (NDVI, NDRE) for every crown.
Finds
Stressed seedlings before leaves visibly wilt. Dead and missing trees. Canopy cover by species.
EGX-10EGX-200

Thermal camera

Measures
Surface temperature of soil and canopy.
Finds
Blocked drip lines and dry emitters, pipe and canal leaks, waterlogging, and trees that have stopped drawing water.
EGX-10EGX-200

Laser scanner (LiDAR)

Measures
3D ground surface and canopy height at centimetre level.
Finds
Tree growth, dune height and movement, erosion gullies, and water flow paths through wadis.
EGX-200EGX-10 compact unit

High-resolution camera

Measures
Visual detail down to 1–3 cm per pixel.
Finds
Photo evidence for each work order. Fence damage, grazing, illegal cutting and encroachment.
All aircraft

Hyperspectral imager

Measures
Hundreds of narrow colour bands per pixel.
Finds
Soil salinity, invasive plants and disease signatures that ordinary cameras cannot separate.
EGX-200

Air, dust & weather probe

Measures
PM2.5 and PM10 dust, temperature, humidity, pressure and wind, at the altitudes flown.
Finds
Dust sources and plume strength. Vertical air profiles for weather and cloud research.

Saudi mission scenarios

Five missions. What the system detects, what operators do, what gets measured.

Tap a number on the map or a tab. Sites are proposed pilot locations.

Madinah Region · Al-Hanakiyah rangeland · 24.9° N 40.5° E

Keep newly planted native trees alive through their first summers

NCVC plants native acacias (Acacia tortilis, Acacia seyal) in protected rangeland such as the King Abdulaziz Protected Pasture in Al-Hanakiyah. Most losses happen in the first hot season, when a blocked drip line or a fence gap can kill a whole row before anyone walks past it.

The system detects

  • Every seedling, located and given a permanent ID
  • Stressed seedlings before leaves wilt, from plant-health and thermal signals
  • Dry rows from blocked or broken drip lines, and leaks that waterlog roots
  • Dead and missing positions, and livestock damage near fence gaps

Operators do

  1. DAY 0 · 06:30–10:00EGX-10 flies the site before the heat of the day.
  2. DAY 0 · AFTERNOONThe NCVC site team receives the map and a ranked list of work orders.
  3. DAY 1–3Crews clear lines, fix leaks, close fences, then replant lost positions.
  4. DAY 21Re-flight confirms recovery; orders close with photo evidence.
  5. MONTHS 6 · 12 · 24Full survival census of every tree.

We measure

Survival rateBy tree, by row and by species, at 6, 12 and 24 months
Detection to repairDays from the flight to the fixed line, per work order
Water per surviving treeLitres delivered ÷ trees alive at each census

Aircraft: EGX-10Sensors: plant-health, thermal, high-res cameraSaudi partners: NCVC, Madinah Region officials

Eastern Province · Al-Ahsa Oasis · 25.4° N 49.6° E

Stop the water losses that nobody sees from the ground

Al-Ahsa holds more than 2.5 million date palms on about 85 km², the world's largest self-contained oasis. Its water comes from the same aquifers the nation depends on. Leaking channels, over-watered blocks and thirsty palms look the same from the road.

The system detects

  • Channel and pipe leaks, which show as cool, wet patches on the thermal map
  • Over-watered and waterlogged blocks, and salt crust on the soil surface
  • Under-watered palms with hot canopies and falling vigour
  • Palm count and canopy health for every farm block

Operators do

  1. WEEK 1EGX-200 flies an oasis-wide thermal and plant-health baseline.
  2. WEEK 2Irrigation teams receive a leak list with coordinates and photos.
  3. WEEK 2–6EGX-10 checks priority blocks; farms get block-level watering advice.
  4. EACH SEASONRepeat survey shows which repairs and schedule changes worked.

We measure

Water per hectareApplied water per block, before and after advice
Leaks closedNumber found, number repaired and confirmed by re-flight
Palm conditionShare of palms in the healthy vigour class, per season

Aircraft: EGX-200 survey, EGX-10 follow-upSensors: thermal, plant-health, LiDAR, high-res cameraSaudi partners: Ministry of Environment, Water and Agriculture; irrigation operators

Hail Region · southern edge of An Nafud · 28.0° N 41.8° E

Measure moving sand and stop it before it buries what the Kingdom builds

Wind drives sand over new plantings, farms, roads and rail lines, and bare disturbed soil releases dust that reaches cities. Stabilisation works such as shelterbelts and sand fences are expensive. Today it is hard to prove which ones are holding.

The system detects

  • Dune height and position to centimetres, from repeated LiDAR scans
  • How far each dune front moved since the last flight, and toward what
  • Bare and disturbed soil patches that act as dust sources
  • Whether sand fences and shelterbelt plantings are still standing and growing

Operators do

  1. BEFORE THE WINDY SEASONEGX-200 maps the corridor and nearby dune field.
  2. WEEK 2Planners rank threatened sections by sand advance and the assets at risk.
  3. MONTHS 1–4Teams build fences and plant shelterbelts at the ranked sections.
  4. AFTER THE WINDY SEASONRe-survey measures the advance at protected and unprotected sections.

We measure

Dune advanceMetres per season, protected vs. unprotected sections
Area stabilisedHectares treated that are still holding after 12 months
Dust at sourcePM10 near treated sources, before and after works

Aircraft: EGX-200Sensors: LiDAR, high-res camera, plant-health, dust & wind probeSaudi partners: NCVC, National Center of Meteorology, road and rail operators

Asir & Al-Baha highlands · 18.2° N 42.5° E

Map juniper dieback tree by tree and supply restoration on roadless slopes

A field study of the southwest found dieback in 11.4% of juniper trees in Asir and 14.5% in Al-Baha. NCVC and park authorities are regenerating these forests, and Soudah Development has planted about 165,000 native trees in the highlands. Steep terrain makes both monitoring and planting slow.

The system detects

  • Each juniper crown classed as healthy, declining or dead
  • Dieback hotspots by slope, elevation and aspect, to guide disease sampling
  • Survival of new seedlings on restoration terraces
  • Grazing damage and broken exclusion fences

Operators do

  1. SURVEYEGX-200 LiDAR and plant-health survey of the forest block; EGX-10 on priority slopes.
  2. WEEK 2Forest teams sample the ranked hotspots on the ground.
  3. PLANTING SEASONThe converted helicopter lifts seedlings, water tanks and fencing to roadless sites.
  4. EVERY YEARRepeat survey tracks decline and seedling survival.

We measure

Crowns in declineShare of junipers declining, trend year on year
Seedling survivalPlanted junipers alive at 12 and 24 months
Logistics savedKilograms delivered by air and crew-hours saved on foot

Aircraft: EGX-200, EGX-10, converted helicopterSensors: LiDAR, plant-health, high-res cameraSaudi partners: NCVC, park authorities, Soudah Development

Riyadh · Qassim · Hail corridor · 26.3° N 44.0° E

Give the national cloud-seeding program more measurements per riyal

The National Center of Meteorology began its cloud-seeding program in 2022 in Riyadh, Hail and Qassim. By late 2024 it had flown 444 flights and more than 1,400 flight hours. Knowing which clouds respond needs more measurements around them, at lower cost and risk than crewed aircraft.

The system measures

  • Vertical profiles of temperature, humidity and pressure below and around target clouds
  • Aerosol and dust load in the air column
  • Wind at flight levels, before and after a seeding pass
  • Dust plume strength during storm events, for forecast checks

Operators do

  1. FORECASTNCM scientists choose the event and approve the flight profile.
  2. EVENT DAYEGX-200 flies the profile before and after the seeding aircraft.
  3. WITHIN HOURSCalibrated data reaches NCM in its own format.
  4. END OF SEASONJoint review of data quality and cost against crewed flights.

We measure

Profiles deliveredUsable vertical profiles per event
Data qualityAgreement with NCM reference instruments
Cost per profileCompared with the same measurement by crewed aircraft

Aircraft: EGX-200Sensors: air, dust & weather probeSaudi partner: National Center of Meteorology

Measured results

Success is counted on the ground, not in flight hours.

Every pilot site starts with a baseline survey. Every result is reported against that baseline and can be checked independently.

Pilot plan

Start in Madinah. Prove it in 12 months.

A focused pilot on three sites, with clear results at each decision gate. Scale-up is decided on evidence.

MONTHS 0–3

Approvals and baseline

  • GACA flight authorizations filed and agreed
  • Site agreements with NCVC and the Ministry
  • Baseline survey of every tree and channel on all three sites
  • Data platform live on in-Kingdom hosting
  • Saudi operator and analyst training starts

Gate 1Baseline maps accepted by the Saudi site owners.

MONTHS 4–9

Operations through summer

  • Scheduled flights on every site, plus on-demand flights after alerts
  • Work orders to field teams, each closed by re-flight
  • Seasonal surveys at Al-Ahsa and the Hail sand corridor
  • Monthly results report to the working group

Gate 2Detection-to-repair cycle working on all sites through the hot season.

MONTHS 10–12

Proof and decision

  • 12-month survival census against baseline
  • Water, sand and cost results per site
  • Independent review of the evidence
  • Scale-up plan: regions, fleet, local support and workforce

Gate 3Saudi decision on national scale-up.

Pilot sites

  • Madinah Region: Al-Hanakiyah native-tree restoration (lead site)
  • Eastern Province: an Al-Ahsa irrigation district
  • Hail Region: a sand-threatened corridor section

Approvals, handled from day one

  • GACA's small-drone rule (GACAR Part 107) covers aircraft under 25 kg. Heavier aircraft and flights beyond the operator's sight need specific GACA authorization.
  • EMYRGEN prepares the full file for GACA: aircraft data, safety case, operating procedures and crew qualifications.

Saudi ownership

  • Control: Saudi teams set priorities and authorize every action
  • Data: hosted in the Kingdom, owned by the program
  • People: Saudi operators, analysts and maintainers trained from month one
  • Industry: a path to local integration, maintenance and support
